title: Toxic Positivity about AI is killing your game - make a game with AI and actually succeed
author: Not-a-Clever-UN
selftext:
Not a brag, just some background on me.  I've worked across a few industries, all tech related, and grew up in the 90s obsessed with tech.  I've worked in business management roles  at a few startups, and in game-dev since 2015. I've got a comp sci degree, a mba, and certificates specifically for small businesses and entrepreneurship (earned as a few extra classes while getting degrees).  

AI *is* like magic... but to the same extent that computers solved accounting by typewriter in the 80s.  It's still just a tool.

I'm flabbergasted by the amount of toxic positivity and defensiveness I see here about AI.  The problem with this mindset is that it blinds you to the flaws that your players WILL spot.  AI has gotten good enough that it *can* produce quality game content, but it doesn't just spit out a polished product.  

So what your choices are:

* Work on a game that AI is specifically good at making.

* Work on your dream game, but put in a lot of effort to fix the limitations and flaws AI presents.

* Work on your dream game, for yourself and a small audience and don't care about how "good" it is or how well it sells.  If you enjoy it and that's the goal, that's valid. 

* Work on your dream game, and put out slop, and be upset it doesn't sell well.  

So what's my advice here?  Be objective.  Know what your end goals are and what you might need to "sacrifice" to reach them.  There's trade-offs in each case.  The outcome I think most people want, which is a polished good "dream game" that sells well, is usually going to require more time and effort than making another decision.   The next best option is to find the limitations of AI, and make a game that takes those into account.  

For example, if you make a model with Tripo, at first it looks pretty good, but if you actually compare it to a modular, customizable character in a first person game, it starts coming up really short.  There's no mouth shapes for speaking animations.  There's blurry spots where the projection sort of just interpolates the texture.  The mouth is fused, there's no tongue, the eyes are fused... 

So what do you do?  Make a game that doesn't need that quality of   character.  So have no NPCs, or go for a low poly style, or make it zoomed out enough...  there's options, but "Skyrim" or "GTA" aren't good ones.   Alternatively, you buy handmade, or AI made and refined by hand, assets that already are set up to do this.  

Likewise, there's other limitations the AI runs into, frequently.  You can bash your head against them, and if you have the endurance, you can probably solve them.  But that's time, effort and money.  If you don't have those resources, and the stamina to keep at it, your next best bet is to scope your game properly.

Anyways, that's my advice, and I hope someone finds it useful.  Feel free to add your own 2cents.
